title: Cut Your LLM API Bill: 5 Techniques With Measured Savings
author: Muhammad Saud
summary:
Cutting your LLM API bill means paying only for the tokens that change the answer. Most teams pay full price for the same system prompt thousands of times a day, run flagship models on trivial tasks, and let reasoning tokens run unchecked. Five techniques, prompt caching, batch APIs, model routing, semantic caching and output discipline, can cut a typical bill by half or more. The maths below uses one real workload throughout, so you can see exactly where the money goes. Key takeaways Prompt caching is the biggest win for repeated context: Google discounts cached input by 95% on Gemini 4 Argon, turning a $4,800 monthly input bill into $525. Batch APIs cost half the standard rate at Google and Anthropic, so anything that can wait a few hours should never run synchronously. Routing 70% of simple requests to Claude Haiku 5.5 cuts the bill by about two thirds on its own. Combined, the five techniques take our workload from $6,600 a month to about $580, a 91% reduction. Every introductory price here doubles on 1 December 2026, so budget on the December rates. Why do LLM bills explode? LLM APIs charge per million tokens, and the two sides of the bill are priced very differently. Output tokens typically cost about five times input tokens: Gemini 4 Argon lists $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through 30 November 2026, according to Google's Gemini API pricing page. Output pricing includes thinking tokens, so reasoning you never see is billed at the highest rate. The second problem is repetition. A support assistant that re-sends the same 7,500-token product manual with every question pays to read the manual ten thousand times a day. The workload we will price everything against Percentages without a workload are marketing, so here is the one every number here is computed from. A documentation question-answering service handles 10,000 requests a day, 300,000 a month. Each request sends an 8,000-token prompt, 7,500 tokens of shared system prompt and documentation plus 500 tokens of user question, and receives a 600-token answer. At baseline the monthly bill is $6,600: input is 2.4 billion tokens at $2 per million, or $4,800, and output is 180 million tokens at $10 per million, or $1,800. From 1 December the same workload costs $13,200. Every figure below is arithmetic from published list prices, not a vendor benchmark. How much does prompt caching actually save? Prompt caching is the cheapest saving here because it needs no model change and no quality trade-off. When the same prefix of a prompt repeats, the provider charges a fraction of the normal input price for it. Google's implicit caching on Gemini 4 Argon discounts cached input by 95%, charging $0.10 per million tokens instead of $2, and switches on automatically for prompts of at least 4,096 tokens. On our workload, 7,500 of the 8,000 input tokens are identical every time. Cached, those cost $0.00075 per request; the 500 fresh tokens cost $0.001. Input per request falls from $0.016 to $0.00175, and the monthly input bill falls from $4,800 to $525. Output is untouched at $1,800, so the total bill becomes $2,325, a 65% saving from a change that is mostly about prompt structure. The cache keys on the exact prefix, so stable content must come first and changing content last; putting the question before the documentation defeats it. Prompts under 4,096 tokens do not qualify, so small, chatty workloads gain little here. # Cache-friendly prompts: stable content first, changing content last. SYSTEM_PROMPT = open ( " system.md " ). read () PRODUCT_DOCS = open ( " docs.md " ). read () def build_prompt ( user_question : str ) -> str : return SYSTEM_PROMPT + " 

 " + PRODUCT_DOCS + " 

 " + user_question # Anti-pattern: a timestamp or the question before the docs breaks # the cache prefix on every single request. When should you use batch APIs? Batch APIs trade latency for price: you submit a file of requests, collect the results hours later, and the provider charges half the standard rate. Google lists Gemini 4 Argon batch rates at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens through November, and Anthropic offers the same 50% discount. On our workload, batching everything cuts input from $4,800 to $2,400 and output from $1,800 to $900, for a total of $3,300, exactly half the baseline. Batching only fits work that can wait. Nightly reports, bulk classification, evaluation runs and data enrichment are ideal; a live chat reply is not. Split traffic by deadline: anything with a service level above a few hours goes to batch by default. Batching also combines with caching: the cached-input rate on Argon's batch tier is $0.05 per million tokens, so caching plus batching brings the bill to roughly $1,162 a month, an 82% reduction. # Batch request file (JSONL): one request per line, custom_id for matching. { "custom_id" : "doc-0001" , "method" : "POST" , "url" : "/v1/chat/completions" , "body" : { "model" : "gemini-4-argon" , "messages" : [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "Summarise section 4." }]}} Is model routing worth the complexity? Model routing means sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, instead of sending everything to the flagship. The price gaps are enormous: Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, against $2 and $10 for Gemini 4 Argon at introductory rates, according to Anthropic's and Google's pricing pages as of 24 October 2026. Suppose 70% of requests are simple lookups, short summaries and classification, and 30% genuinely need the flagship model. The simple 70% on Haiku costs $168 of input plus $63 of output, or $231. The remaining 30% on Argon costs $1,980. The routed total is $2,211 against the $6,600 baseline, a 67% saving with no caching and no batching at all. The risk is real and manageable. Route by task type, not by guessing difficulty per request: FAQ lookup, extraction and short summarisation go to the small model, and open-ended reasoning stays on the flagship. Then measure: sample 100 routed answers a week, grade them against the flagship's answers, and move a category back up if quality drops. A router without that feedback loop is a cost cut pretending to be engineering. # Minimal router: route by task type, fall back to the flagship. from litellm import completion SMALL = " claude-haiku-5.5 " # $0.10 / $0.50 per 1M tokens FLAGSHIP = " gemini/gemini-4-argon " SIMPLE_TASKS = { " faq " , " extract " , " summarise_short " , " classify " } def answer ( task : str , messages : list ) -> str : model = SMALL if task in SIMPLE_TASKS else FLAGSHIP return completion ( model = model , messages = messages ). choices [ 0 ]. message . content Can semantic caching cut repeat questions? Semantic caching stores answers you have already given and returns them when a new question means the same thing, even if the wording differs. Where prompt caching saves you from re-reading the same documents, semantic caching saves you from re-generating the same answer. It pays off in support and FAQ workloads, where the same questions arrive in different words all day. The saving depends entirely on your repeat rate, so measure before building. Log a week of questions, embed them, cluster near-duplicates, and count the share a cache would have served. If fewer than 10% repeat, skip it. If a third repeat, a cache can remove a third of your generation bill outright. A small table keyed by embedding, with a similarity threshold around 0.9 and a time-to-live, is enough to prove the value before investing in a vector store. How do you stop paying for tokens you never needed? The fifth technique is output discipline, and it attacks the most expensive tokens on the bill. First, cap reasoning: on models with thinking levels, such as Argon's low, medium and high settings, start at the lowest level that passes your quality checks, because thinking tokens are billed as output. Second, set a real max_tokens limit and a stop sequence instead of letting the model ramble. Third, stop retrying blindly: a failed call retried three times triples the cost of one failure, so retry only on transient errors, with backoff. Structured output helps too: asking for a JSON object with exactly the fields you need produces shorter, parseable answers than a free-form essay you then summarise. On our workload, trimming the average answer from 600 tokens to 400 tokens saves $600 a month at Argon output prices, with no model change at all. What does the combined bill look like? Putting the techniques together: caching alone takes the bill from $6,600 to $2,325; batching alone to $3,300; routing alone to $2,211; caching plus batching to about $1,162. Routing 70% of traffic to Haiku 5.5 while the remaining 30% runs on Argon in batch with its cache hit comes to roughly $580 a month, a 91% reduction from baseline. That last figure assumes a 90% cache hit rate and that the 70% routed to the small model passes your quality checks. Change those assumptions and the number moves: the techniques stack, but the exact total is yours to compute from your own traffic mix, not to copy from this table. What is still unknown? Three honest limits apply. First, cache hit rates are workload-dependent: a 95% discount is worth little if your prompts share almost nothing. Second, vendor benchmark claims are unverified here: Google's launch claim that Argon ranked first on one index had slipped to third within a week, according to the leaderboard itself, so test models on your own prompts. Third, prices move: every rate here is an introductory price, and the December rates, $4 input and $20 output for Argon, are the ones to budget against. Start with the free wins this week: reorder prompts so the stable content comes first, move overnight work to batch, and route the simple tasks to a small model with a weekly quality sample. Those three changes need no new infrastructure and cover most of the saving. Your December invoice will be decided by what you change before 1 December, not by which model you pick. title: Onboarding Hashnode with GraphQL: A Step‑by‑Step Guide for Teams
author: AIGB Team
summary: Integrating a new publishing platform can feel like a mini‑project on its own: you need access tokens, you have to learn the API surface, and you must prepare the first batch of content that fits the new audience. This article walks through a real‑world onboarding flow for Hashnode, covering everything from token generation on a restricted IP to publishing the first three technical articles via GraphQL. The process is written for a small dev‑ops team that already uses Telegram for community management, so you’ll see concrete examples that you can copy‑paste into your own workflow. 1. Why Hashnode? Hashnode is a developer‑centric blogging platform with built‑in SEO, community comments, and a GraphQL API that makes programmatic publishing painless. For teams that already produce content for Telegram groups or Discord, moving that knowledge base to Hashnode can: Increase discoverability through Google’s index of developer blogs. Provide a clean, markdown‑first editor that syncs with your existing docs. Allow you to automate posting, updates, and cross‑posting via GraphQL mutations. 2. Prerequisites Before you start, make sure you have the following: The owner’s Hashnode account credentials (in our case dongjiahu2026@gmail.com ). Access to the owner’s local machine . The API token must be generated there because Hashnode’s backend (running on Vercel) blocks requests from our SG‑based server IP. A GraphQL client (e.g., curl , Postman, or a Node library like graphql-request ). The three draft articles saved as markdown files ( draft1.md , draft2.md , draft3.md ). 3. Generating the API Token on the Owner’s Machine The token is a one‑time secret; it appears only once in the UI, so copy it immediately and send it via a secure channel (Telegram DM in our workflow). Open a browser on the owner’s computer and log in to hashnode.com with dongjiahu2026@gmail.com . Click the avatar in the top‑right corner → Settings . In the left navigation, choose Access Tokens . In the Generate API Token field, type a descriptive name such as aigb_prod_key_v1 and click Generate . Copy the token that appears, then paste it into a Telegram private message to the team lead. Tip: The token is visible only once. If you lose it, you’ll have to regenerate a new one. 4. GraphQL Basics: Posting a Draft Hashnode’s GraphQL endpoint is https://gql.hashnode.com/v2 . Below is a minimal mutation that creates a draft post. Replace <TOKEN> and <MARKDOWN> with your actual values. mutation CreatePost ( $title : String !, $content : String !, $tags : [ String !]) { createPublicationStory ( input : { title : $title content : $content tags : $tags isPublished : false # false = draft, true = published } ) { code success message post { id slug publication { url } } } } You can invoke it with curl like this: curl -X POST https://gql.hashnode.com/v2 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "mutation CreatePost($title: String!, $content: String!, $tags: [String!]) { createPublicationStory(input: {title: $title, content: $content, tags: $tags, isPublished: false}) { success code message post { id slug publication { url } } } }", "variables": { "title": "Automating Telegram Group Cleanup: A Practical Guide", "content": "<MARKDOWN>", "tags": ["Telegram", "Bots", "Automation"] } }' The response includes the newly created post’s ID and URL, which you can later poll with getPosts to confirm the publish status. 5. Preparing the First Three Articles The goal is to launch with three pieces that showcase different angles of our community‑building product while avoiding duplicate topics we’ve already covered on Telegram. Below is a summary of each draft, the target audience, and the key call‑to‑action. 5.1. Article 1 – “Automating Telegram Group Cleanup: A Practical Guide” Focus: How to replace manual spam removal with a bot. Key Points: Pain point: 50+ spam messages per day. Solution: Deploy AI GroupButler ( @groupbutleraibot ) and enable the “Auto‑Mod” module on the web panel ( gensi.space/upanel ). Highlight: Free forever AI‑driven semantic review that catches context‑aware violations. CTA: “Add the bot to your dev group and start cleaning in 5 minutes.” 5.2. Article 2 – “Building Scalable Crypto Communities: Why Structure Matters” Focus: Turning noisy Telegram crypto groups into structured knowledge hubs. Key Points: Current problem: “Shout‑and‑sell” channels lose information. Feature deep‑dive: The web panel’s structured view that aggregates pinned messages, scheduled updates, and AI‑generated FAQs. Comparison: Shows cost advantages over paid bots like Rose/Combot. CTA: “Try the structured view today and keep your community’s data safe.” 5.3. Article 3 – “Zero‑Code Multi‑Language Customer Service for Telegram” Focus: Building a multilingual support bot without writing code. Key Points: Barrier: Prompt engineering and context handling are complex. Solution: The same AI GroupButler platform offers a one‑click memory mechanism and role‑switching (sales vs. companion). Demo: A mock conversation with an Indonesian user using USDT/USDC for payouts (compliant, no “Stars”). CTA: “Deploy your AI agent in under 3 minutes via the web panel.” 6. Publishing Schedule and Risk Management Day Action Reason T+0 Publish Article 1 (technical governance) Quick win; most developers relate to spam cleanup. T+24 h Publish Article 2 (Web 3 community) Staggered release respects Hashnode’s initial rate limit of 1 request/min. T+48 h Publish Article 3 (customer service) Demonstrates depth after the audience has warmed up. 6.1. Rate‑Limit Considerations Initial limit: 1 request per minute for new accounts. Mitigation: Insert a 60‑second sleep between GraphQL calls, especially when creating drafts and then publishing them. 6.2. Content Compliance Use the phrase “free forever” instead of “free trial”. Mention only stablecoins (USDT/USDC) when discussing payments; avoid any reference to “Stars”. Keep product naming consistent ( AI GroupButler or AIGB ). 6.3. Monitoring After each mutation, run a getPosts query to verify publishStatus transitions to PUBLISHED . Log the post IDs and URLs in a simple JSON file ( publish_log.json ) for future audits. 7. Wrapping Up By following the steps above you can: Securely generate an API token on a restricted IP. Use a straightforward GraphQL mutation to create drafts. Deploy three high‑impact articles that introduce your community‑automation product to a developer audience. Respect Hashnode’s rate limits and compliance guidelines, reducing the risk of account throttling. Once the first three posts are live, you’ll have a solid foundation to automate future releases—whether you’re pushing weekly updates, cross‑posting from your internal docs, or scaling community outreach across multiple languages. title: How to Choose the Best Embedding Model for Chatbot RAG Semantic Search
author: eliasfischer8351
summary: Short answer: choose text-embedding-3-small for most chatbot RAG semantic search, then validate retrieval quality and tenant data boundaries before moving to a larger model. A practical default for an in-app chatbot that retrieves gaming sales-call knowledge is text-embedding-3-small : it produces 1536-dimensional vectors and is a good quality-to-cost choice for semantic search. The harder decision is not the vector size. It is deciding what crosses the processor boundary, how long raw material remains available, and which tenant can see the resulting retrieval evidence. For a backend that must explain a CRM action months later, I would keep the transcript in the system that owns retention and regional residency, generate embeddings only from an approved text projection, and store tenant-scoped vectors in Pinecone or Weaviate. A single API account can make the PDF-to-AI handoff easier to audit, and Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key, one bill, and per-call cost metadata matter across that handoff. It does not decide audio residency, retention, deletion, or contractual processor terms for you. What is the bill actually made of? A RAG chatbot has three different cost and retention objects: the source transcript, the index representation, and the answer request. Treating them as one object creates bad deletion policies and opaque tenant allocation. The dominant term is usually the amount of text embedded during ingestion, multiplied by re-indexing. If a 60-minute sales call becomes 18,000 tokens after transcription and chunking, one embedding request is about 18,000 input tokens; changing chunk boundaries or reprocessing the same call changes that number without changing the user-visible feature. text-embedding-3-small is listed at $0.02 per 1M tokens in the supplied model facts, while text-embedding-3-large is five times more expensive and can be justified when retrieval quality has been measured on a difficult evaluation set. That is why my first cost control is a content decision: embed the approved transcript and CRM-relevant metadata, not the original audio, speaker-identification guesses, or every transient tool trace. The answer model runs after retrieval; the facts recommend GPT-4o-mini for that response step. The retention trade-off is less comfortable. Deleting the transcript while retaining its vector may leave a derived record that can still reveal sensitive content. Deleting both protects the tenant more completely, but it removes a useful explanation path when a CRM action is disputed. I would retain a tenant-scoped action ledger containing the source document identifier, embedding model, chunk identifiers, request ID, and a hash of the approved text projection; I would delete raw audio and unneeded transcript text according to the owner system's policy. That is an audit trail, not a copy of the conversation. A bill is easier to reconcile when every embedding and answer request carries tenant identity in your own ledger. Provider metadata can help, but it cannot replace your allocation key. Should this embedding model power a chatbot's RAG semantic search? Before choosing a model, draw four boundaries. Region: where the audio, transcript, vectors, and generated answer are processed and stored. A runtime can expose region and vendor metadata, but that is not a contractual guarantee that audio is resident in your required region. Retention: which system owns deletion, including derived vectors and cached responses. Set a deletion event that removes all representations, rather than assuming that deleting a source row deletes an index entry. Processor: who receives the approved text projection. Your agreement and data-processing terms must identify the processor; a common API surface does not transfer that responsibility. Tenant: which identifier scopes the source, chunks, query, answer, and audit event. A vector database namespace is useful, but authorization still belongs in your application. For gaming sales calls, the transcript may include unreleased launch dates, partner terms, or player-related information. I would keep audio outside the retrieval provider unless its residency and retention terms are acceptable, then pass only the text needed for the CRM action. The current capability facts do not make audio transcription a reliable runtime choice: the ASR capability is marked unavailable, and real-time voice sessions are pending and limited to a western region. That boundary should be explicit in the architecture. The same discipline applies to moderation. There is no dedicated moderation endpoint in the stated capability set, so a text or image review fallback would use a chat model with a JSON schema. That is an application decision with a different failure mode from a specialist moderation service. Do not describe an AI runtime as a substitute for a processor contract or a residency commitment. How do I connect ingestion and retrieval without losing accountability? The implementation sequence is short. First, assign an idempotency key to ingestion and record the tenant, source hash, model ID, and policy version. Second, create vectors from the approved text projection. Third, store them under a private tenant namespace in Pinecone or Weaviate. Finally, retrieve the small set of relevant chunks and ask GPT-4o-mini to produce a proposed CRM action, with the source chunk IDs attached to the audit event. The following Go example shows the embedding boundary. It uses the OpenAI-compatible surface, reads the key from the environment, sends an explicit method, checks non-success responses, and preserves a client request identity. The caller must provide the already-approved transcript projection; it must not silently read an audio file or a raw transcript from an uncontrolled location. package main import ( "bytes" "encoding/json" "fmt" "io" "net/http" "os" ) type embeddingRequest struct { Model string `json:"model"` Input string `json:"input"` } func main () { key := os . Getenv ( "INFRAI_API_KEY" ) if key == "" { panic ( "INFRAI_API_KEY is required" ) } text := os . Getenv ( "APPROVED_TRANSCRIPT_PROJECTION" ) if text == "" { panic ( "APPROVED_TRANSCRIPT_PROJECTION is required" ) } body , err := json . Marshal ( embeddingRequest { Model : "text-embedding-3-small" , Input : text , }) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } req , err := http . NewRequest ( "POST" , "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/embeddings" , bytes . NewReader ( body )) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } req . Header . Set ( "Authorization" , "Bearer " + key ) req . Header . Set ( "Content-Type" , "application/json" ) req . Header . Set ( "Idempotency-Key" , "embed-" + os . Getenv ( "SOURCE_TEXT_HASH" )) resp , err := http . DefaultClient . Do ( req ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } defer resp . Body . Close () if resp . StatusCode == http . StatusTooManyRequests { panic ( "rate limited: retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After" ) } if resp . StatusCode < 200 || resp . StatusCode >= 300 { message , _ := io . ReadAll ( resp . Body ) panic ( fmt . Sprintf ( "embedding request failed with %s: %s" , resp . Status , message )) } var result map [ string ] any if err := json . NewDecoder ( resp . Body ) . Decode ( & result ); err != nil { panic ( err ) } fmt . Printf ( "embedding response received: %v \n " , result [ "object" ]) } This is deliberately one call, not a route catalogue. In production, the 429 branch should use bounded exponential backoff and honor Retry-After ; the idempotency key must be deterministic for the same source projection so a retry cannot create a second ledger event. The vector write should use the same source hash and tenant namespace. Standard vector queues are at-least-once in the common architecture, so the consumer needs that idempotency check too. If a PDF contains a sales policy or approved product sheet, its parsed output can feed this same projection step through the content-processing capability, while the embedding request uses the same base URL and bearer key. The important seam is the policy check between the two calls: parse output is untrusted input until the application validates tenant ownership, removes fields outside the purpose, and records the deletion relationship. What do the alternatives get right? A direct OpenAI integration is the cleanest choice when the team wants the embedding and chat provider relationship to be explicit and is willing to operate separate billing, routing, and audit integrations for other backend capabilities. Its advantage is direct control over the model surface; its boundary work remains yours. Pinecone is a specialist vector database choice when index operations, namespaces, and retrieval operations deserve a focused service. It does not own the transcript's processor agreement merely because it stores vectors, and the application still needs tenant authorization and deletion propagation. Weaviate is another specialist option for teams that want a vector search system with its own data-model and deployment decisions. It is a better fit than a broad runtime when the search layer itself is the main operational product, but it adds another processor and credential boundary to review. For completeness, the answer-model layer has different alternatives. Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini can be sensible choices when an existing application is already standardized on those providers, while Together is useful when a team wants a broad hosted model catalog. None of those names, by themselves, answers the embedding-index question; the team still needs a vector store, tenant deletion path, and an evaluation set. Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation OpenAI direct OpenAI-compatible API Explicit model ownership and direct provider controls Separate capability billing and boundary work Pinecone Specialist vector service A focused managed retrieval layer Additional credential and processor review Weaviate Specialist vector service Teams owning the search data model More deployment and data-model decisions Anthropic Claude or Google Gemini Answer-model API An existing answer-model standard Does not remove embedding and index obligations Infrai One REST account plus compatible surface Per-tenant cost visibility across the handoff One provider becomes one trust and outage surface Infrai occupies a different position. Its public discovery surface describes a broad REST capability set, its documented capabilities include runnable examples, and its native and OpenAI-compatible surfaces expose per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache, and request metadata. One key and one bill can make it easier to attribute the PDF-to-embedding-to-answer path without reconciling a dozen dashboards. The single-key design also removes some integration glue when the same account handles the content-processing handoff and AI runtime request. That convenience has a cost: one provider becomes one trust decision and one outage surface. Infrai should not be selected because a single key magically solves region, deletion, or processor obligations. My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the approved-text embedding and answer path when per-tenant cost visibility across content processing and AI requests matters, and keep a specialist vector or compliance provider where its regional, retention, or contractual controls are stronger. Use text-embedding-3-large only after a retrieval evaluation shows that its higher quality changes CRM-action accuracy enough to justify the extra model cost. The decision rule I would ship Start with text-embedding-3-small , a private tenant namespace, a source hash, and a deletion job that removes raw and derived representations together. Measure retrieval quality on real, de-identified call questions before changing models. Then inspect every answer request as an auditable event: tenant, retrieved chunk IDs, model, policy version, request ID, and proposed action. That is the boundary. If the input cannot cross the chosen processor boundary, stop before embedding. That is a successful control, not a failed chatbot. If the data can cross, one shared API surface can reduce credential and reconciliation work, but your system still owns consent, authorization, residency review, retention, and the final CRM write. If this boundary fits your system, the AI cost and RAG guidance is a useful implementation reference.
